lesson.title: 128 Bits for Everyone: Why the Internet Needed a New IP Version
lesson.summary: IPv6 is the successor to IPv4 at the network layer, expanding addresses from 32 to 128 bits to solve address exhaustion while also simplifying header processing and building in features IPv4 only bolted on later.
lesson.body:
Every device that gets an IP address, and every router that operates at the network layer forwarding packets based on those addresses, was originally designed around IPv4's 32-bit address space, which tops out at roughly 4.3 billion possible addresses, 2 to the 32nd power. That sounds enormous until you account for the explosion of phones, laptops, servers, IoT sensors, and cloud instances that all need their own address; by the early 2010s the pool of unallocated IPv4 addresses was effectively exhausted at the regional registry level. IPv6 is the Internet Engineering Task Force's answer to that exhaustion, standardized to replace IPv4 as the network layer's addressing scheme with a vastly larger space: 128 bits per address instead of 32.

The scale difference is hard to overstate. 2 to the 128th power is approximately 3.4 times 10 to the 38th power, a number so large that even generous, wasteful address assignment policies, handing every single human on Earth a /64 subnet with roughly 18 quintillion addresses of their own, would consume only a tiny fraction of the total space. This was a deliberate design choice: rather than repeating IPv4's history of scarcity and complex workarounds, IPv6's designers wanted enough headroom that address exhaustion would never again be a practical concern, freeing network design from constantly rationing addresses.

IPv6 is not simply IPv4 with longer addresses bolted on; it reworks the network layer more broadly. The header format was redesigned to be simpler and consistently sized, dropping several fields that IPv4 carried but modern networks rarely used, which speeds up router processing since routers no longer need to parse a variable-length options field on every packet by default. IPv6 also builds address autoconfiguration in as a first-class feature rather than an add-on, so a device can generate a usable address for itself in many cases without a DHCP server. Each of these changes is covered in its own right in the concepts that follow this one, but they all stem from the same underlying goal: use the lessons learned from IPv4's decades of operation to build a cleaner, larger, more self-sufficient protocol.

IPv6 addresses are written very differently from IPv4's familiar dotted-decimal form. Instead of four decimal octets, an IPv6 address is written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits, separated by colons, for example 2001:0db8:0000:0000:0000:ff00:0042:8329. That format, and the rules for shortening it, are significant enough to warrant their own dedicated treatment in the very next section on IPv6 address format, but it is worth noting here that this is the same fundamental idea as an IPv4 address, a fixed-length binary number used to identify a device at the network layer, just with more bits and a different, hexadecimal-based human-readable notation.

Adoption of IPv6 has been gradual rather than a single cutover, precisely because IPv4 and IPv6 are not directly interoperable at the packet level; a router or host has to explicitly support both, or rely on translation, to communicate across the two. That gradual, coexistence-heavy transition, including dual-stack operation and tunneling techniques, is exactly what the later concepts in this unit address once the mechanics of IPv6 addressing itself are established here.
